PHSCS 587

Bipolar injection and storage

From the figure to the concept

Fig. 1 shows how injected electrons cross a base while some recombine or remain stored

The same minority-carrier physics appears in a bipolar transistor. In forward-active operation of an NPN device, the emitter–base junction is forward biased and the base–collector junction is reverse biased. Electrons injected from the n-type emitter become minority carriers in the p-type base. A sufficiently thin base allows many to diffuse to the collector depletion region, whose field sweeps them onward.

Some injected electrons recombine in the base, and hole injection into the emitter also contributes to base-current requirements. Using positive terminal-current magnitudes in the usual forward-active convention, IE = IC + IB. Define common-base gain α = IC/IE and common-emitter gain β = IC/IB; then β = α/(1 − α). These ratios summarize terminal behavior rather than replacing the transport and recombination model.

Injected minority charge is stored in the device. Switching conditions must change that charge as well as terminal voltage, so lifetime, diffusion distance and junction bias history affect speed. Deep saturation forward biases both junctions and can add stored charge. This gives context for comparing a majority-carrier Schottky contact with a minority-injecting PN structure under specified operating conditions.

Example

If an illustrative forward-active transistor has α = 0.98, its corresponding current ratio is β = 49. Achieving that ratio depends on injection efficiency, base transport and recombination, rather than on terminal algebra alone.

Practice

1. Why does making the base thin relative to a minority diffusion length help collection?

Compare transit distance with recombination loss.

Injected electrons can reach the collector-side depletion region with a smaller chance of recombining in the base.

2. What physical state must be tracked to predict switching after substantial injection?

Consider carriers already present.

The stored excess carrier distribution must be tracked or approximated. Terminal voltages alone do not specify how quickly that charge leaves.
